title: Midori Takada – Through The Looking Glass (1983) - 45rpy
text:
“Why do Westerners need to have so many instruments?” (an African drummer to Midori Takada)
I probably already knew some of these things about ambient music, but reading the notes to this recently gifted record will hopefully orientate me for this, my third listen. Midori Takada, primarily a percussionist, saw her first solo album as a conscious countermove to the prevailing aggression and virtuosity of Western music (coming just short of characterizing European classical as war-making music). Takada’s approach is more inward-facing, rather than expressive. While I’m turned off by ostentation in music, emotion at least is often a desired consequence (I spent the morning playing The Zombies, and what sounds could be more demonstrative than that?). I’m guilty of ghettoizing some music in my habits of listening, relegating certain records as background to a simultaneous activity—and the term ‘ambient’ effectively does the same thing—but I am now attempting full, mindful engagement…
I suppose the bird-like whistles I can pick out from her ethereal soundscape are vaguely ‘Japanese,’ but from the first track “Mr. Henri Rousseau’s Dream” and LP cover art—both in homage to that Naïve painter—to the flurry of African rhythms that conclude the album, I sense something that is at least Eurafrican in scope. Takada’s practice is effectively improvisation with herself, augmenting each pass of analog tape with fresh, minimal instrumentation. The contribution of each component is sometimes hard to discern, like bells so gently played that their resonance could be almost anything. The opening clang of “Crossing” more clearly conjures a ferry, soon augmented by Takada’s polyrhythmic marimba, and is almost purely percussive, apart from a judicious drone of a harmonium. The wind sounds (played on a Coke bottle) of “Trompe-l’œil” arouse exotic jungle birds, with a reed organ the only moderately civilizing force (and though the track title suggests a wider dimensional space, it’s one of the flatter sounding pieces to these ears).
The densely packed closer “Catastrophe Σ” brings most of the previously used instrumentation together, and the addition of skinned drums make for the most human articulation of Takada’s craft. Here the inward/outward distinction becomes more nebulous and a bit suspect to me. At the mid-point of the 15-minute piece, there is a signal—a carillon call if you will—for a dramatic shift and it’s difficult not to think, at least once, of the thunderous drums as war-like. It all hums along rather than builds and before anything like a crescendo, either the playing all comes to a hard stop or there’s an abrupt cut to the ‘performance’—a word I imagine Takada might shun. But she’s asked us to listen, and I’ll meet her half way by conceding the record is beautifully compelling without being overly commanding. Which is to say when I began to feel idle I started the seasonal business of wrapping gifts and packing bags and came the conclusion that I’d take the ringing chimes of Takada over sleigh bells any time of year.

title: Seeds, Leaves and Metal Chopsticks: Making Music with Midori Takada | Red Bull Music Academy Daily
text:
Seeds, Leaves and Metal Chopsticks: Making Music with Midori Takada
The experimental Japanese composer and percussionist on her distinct sonic approach
An elusive Japanese composer, percussionist and sometimes actress, Midori Takada has been recording her unique twist on minimalism for over four decades. After releasing two albums in the early ’80s with the Mkwaju Ensemble, a Japanese group of artists who took their name from the Swahili word for “drumming,” Takada went solo and released her 1983 album Through the Looking Glass. That album was reissued to widespread acclaim in 2017 and led to a resurgence of interest in her work, with Takada finally finding her rightful place in the canon of minimalist composers.
In these edited and condensed excerpts from her Fireside Chat with Frosty on Red Bull Radio, the avant-garde artist discusses the early inspirations that were formative to her musical journey and how to make music with unorthodox materials.
Where were you born? How was music part of your early life?
I was born in Tokyo soon after the second war, so people were poor then. But that was normal life at the [time] for people, so everybody after the war, everybody [was the] same.
Is there something about the equilibrium that you think was a good thing? Sometimes you use your imagination and you start to dream more.
Yes. I was always [very imaginative]. So my heart wasn’t there, [but] my brain was playing in a different world from very young.
Was there a sonic component to the imagination or was that not a part of it?
No, no sonic imagination, but my mother played piano every day, she was teacher of piano. And my father was teaching in high school and after that university – he taught English literature, so he gave me lots of books.
What types of songs did your mother play on the piano?
Chopin, Bach and Beethoven. Every day she played piano beside my bed.
Did you find yourself playing with the piano? Did you find yourself exploring?
Not exploring – my mother taught me first. But I was always against it, so my mother took me to a different teacher.
I played many materials – grass, stones, irons, or sometimes seeds of plants or leaves of trees. It felt natural to me.
When did you start playing professionally?
After graduating I worked as a professional musician. I worked with many fine artists and sculptors. I played their sound installations; in the ’80s artists were doing a lot of collaborations with sound and art.
When you’re looking at a sculpture, is there usually a first space on it that you want to explore? And what tools do you use to interact with the sculpture?
Yes, many. Sometimes I’d hit a glass bowl to them, or I’d hit it with mallets or bars of iron. Once I played a big iron sculpture, it was three meters or four meters high, built on the lakeside. I put speakers on a boat and the boat on the opposite side of the lake sculpture. I played one side of the sculpture and on the other side was the boat with speakers, so my sound spread wide and the sound came back softened by the water. The sound on the water becomes very soft with a little bit of vibration from the water. It was a beautiful, improvised moment.
When you were doing these collaborations you were already spending your life in sound and music. Was there a moment earlier when you realized how powerful sound is?
I didn’t have the confidence for improvised music because I was trained playing written composed music. But yes, there was one day I played with jazz musicians at a time when the music scene was deconstructed [free jazz]. Before that I played many materials – grass, stones, irons, or sometimes seeds of plants or leaves of trees. It felt natural to me.
Who were some of the musicians that you found exciting to play with?
My group Ton-Klami. Ton-Klami means “circle” in Korean. We two countries [Japan and Korea] have always had a cultural exchange, like the circle. It also means money, so Ton-Klami is “to be without money.” Without money we play, so I named the group Ton-Klami. Masahiko Satoh is a very excellent jazz piano player and a composer and he was involved in free jazz from the ’60s, and Kang Tae Hwan is a saxophonist from Korea and he has circular breath. I play different things depending on the venue, or country, or city. I sometimes find materials for playing, so sometimes the bucket in the dressing room, I’ll bring it to the stage.
You’ve played a lot of vibraphone, xylophones and similar instruments. When did you first start playing these instruments and why did that sound or the structure appeal to you over other instruments?
First, I’m interested in human history, and the keyboard, like a xylophone, marimba, etc... started in the B.C. era. It started out with human beings playing just one bar. One day they found two tones. They noticed the difference of the two tones, which was a very important thing. After that, they dug in the ground and put two bars on it on the floor. Now the floor had resonance. Then they found the scales and after that it spread all over the world. In Africa they found different materials, like bamboo – in Madagascar they made it by bamboo. But in a scale it’s very similar in intonation to the Columbian scale. It’s very interesting how similar it is because the origin is Eastern.
As you’re playing the marimba, it sounds like it’s more than just the sound that is appealing to you – that you’re connecting to human heritage when you’re playing something like this. Do you feel it is part of that continuum? The connection with the ancestors around the world?
Yes, it’s a part of my reason for playing.
How did the Mkwaju Ensemble come about and what was your mission or your focus to explore that group?
So, it was the ’70s after having graduated university. I wanted to make a special group for playing minimal music, because there were many percussion ensembles, but they play a very westernized music and that attitude for playing is quite different. Minimal music is, I have thought, requires a very controlled mind. Controlled technique to keep the sound. Not emotional, but like meditation that the audience can receive as they like.
To put the audience in a meditative space.
Space, and for the player to have to control very calmly and keep tones very precisely. Not weak, but not too strong. It’s very special training we need. It’s a very different type of ensemble. I needed members for that. It was very famous.
Was this group first for live performances or was it for studio recordings?
Studio. Live is difficult. It needs money. Lots of money. Recording was the first work. Before that, we trained.
The music that was on the first Mkwaju album – what was the basis of that music?
I chose traditional music from Africa – the Gogo tribe and Zanaki tribe of Tanzania. It comes from a vivid atmosphere. Sometimes I felt people talking. Sometimes a dog barking or wind blowing. I felt all of their environment, then I played the solo. I arranged for the marimbaphone – westernized marimbaphone. After that, Joe Hisaishi arranged it for a trio, then Nippon Columbia recorded it and made a binaural.
Did you try to create any sort of environment in the studio to emphasize these elements? Was it important for listeners to feel like they connected with your environment through the recording?
Environment is very important because of the culture. For resonance in Africa, they use the gourd. Gourd, and the spider’s nest for booster... People’s knowledge and enlightenment has to come from environment and life.
It’s an instrument, and music is including everything of Earth’s culture. It’s very important to [be able to] see instruments. One instrument comes in many forms.
When you recorded Through the Looking Glass, you were using traditional instruments, but also you were using materials that were non-traditional. Was Through the Looking Glass your experience going through life and your surroundings?
Yes. It’s made from [the] concept of time. The materials are used from my career. I found some materials. Many bells from India, or Japanese bells, horse bells. And in Bali island, I found some wooden materials, and bamboo flute. I was playing with [the idea of] hearing my past, face to face.
Through the Looking Glass in the past couple of years has taken on a new life with the reissue. Do you feel like you’ve evolved in a different way, or does that album still feel like a natural expression of who you are today?
I didn’t notice the [resurgence in interest] because I don’t like any social media and normally I don’t listen to my recorded music after its recorded.
Why do you choose not to listen to it?
I gave all my concentration to make it and after that I was empty for a while.
Are you frequently listening to music? You’ve said you don’t listen to your own music much, except in the moment as you’re creating and performing. Are you avidly listening to other music?
Not modern music. But I listen to recorded music from other time periods. I don’t listen to music in my home, I just play. I play and make sound, that’s most important for me. Using my body is important, so using my body and feeling materials or vibrations and the sound it makes makes me brave to do something next.
Is there an instrument that is most important to you in this world?
A metal chopstick. It has great sound and is very light. If you just swing it like chimes by a window or even just a little touch with a finger, it makes sound.
What do you hope people get from your music when they hear it?
It’s up to you. Music is free to receive and how you receive it is free, because music is something nobody could own.

title: Midori Takada — Grokipedia
text:
Midori Takada
Biography
Early Life and Education
Midori Takada was born on December 21, 1951, in Tokyo, Japan. Her mother worked as a piano teacher, providing Takada with early exposure to music in a cosmopolitan household. Takada began piano lessons around age three at her parents' insistence, though she initially detested them despite incentives like cookies; by age six, she was independently picking out Chopin chords.[3][6] Takada pursued higher education in music at Tokyo University of the Arts (Tokyo Geijutsu Daigaku), where she received classical training as a percussionist. She graduated in 1974, focusing on percussion techniques that would inform her later compositional style.[3][7]Formation and Activities of Mkwaju Ensemble
Midori Takada founded the Mkwaju Ensemble in the early 1980s as a percussion-centric group exploring minimalist compositions infused with African rhythmic elements and Eastern instrumentation.[5][8] The ensemble's core members included Takada on marimba, vibraphone, gong, and tom-tom; Yoji Sadanari on bass marimba, gong, and tom-tom; and Junko Arase on mitla marimba and gong, with keyboard support from Joe Hisaishi and Masahiro Miwa.[9] Hisaishi, who produced the group's recordings, contributed to the integration of subtle electronic textures alongside acoustic percussion.[10][11] The ensemble's primary activities centered on studio recordings that emphasized repetitive patterns and polyrhythms, yielding two albums in 1981 on the Better Days label: the self-titled Mkwaju, recorded on February 6–7 and March 12, and released in June; and Ki-Motion, issued later that year.[10][12][13] These works featured extended tracks like the 12-minute "Flash-Back" on Mkwaju, showcasing layered percussion and ambient swells that prefigured Takada's later solo explorations.[14] The group's output drew from Takada's percussion training and influences such as West African drumming traditions, adapted into a Japanese minimalist framework without electronic overproduction.[15][8] Financial constraints led to the ensemble's disbandment after these releases, limiting its activities to these recordings rather than extensive touring or further projects.[16] Despite the short tenure, the albums gained cult status for their innovative fusion, influencing subsequent ambient and fourth-world music scenes, with reissues in 2018 by WRWTFWW Records highlighting their enduring appeal.[8][17]Breakthrough with Through the Looking Glass
Through the Looking Glass is Midori Takada's debut solo album, released in 1983 by RCA Japan, marking her transition from ensemble work to individual compositional expression.[18][19] Recorded over two days at Aoyama Studio in Tokyo on analog tape, Takada self-produced and mixed the album using a limited setup including marimbas, gongs, chimes, recorders, reed organ (harmonium), and unconventional elements like Coca-Cola bottles for percussion effects.[19][18] She employed overdubbing and improvisation to build layered, repetitive patterns, measuring microphone distances to sculpt a three-dimensional sonic space.[19] The album consists of four tracks: "Mr. Henri Rousseau's Dream" (11:15), featuring marimba, gongs, and chimes in a hypnotic, minimalist pulse; "Crossing" (9:15), incorporating polyrhythms with cowbell, marimba, and harmonium inspired by Japanese train crossing bells; "Trompe-l'œil" (6:00), a playful piece with harmonium and bottle tones evoking optical illusions; and "Catastrophe Σ" (15:00), an intense percussion-driven finale with tom-toms, bongos, cymbals, and piano accents building to rhythmic complexity.[18][20] Takada drew from African drumming traditions, Asian gamelan and koto elements, and Western minimalists like Steve Reich and Terry Riley, creating contemplative, infinity-evoking soundscapes that prioritized physicality and time over electronic precision.[19][18][21] At release, the album received limited attention in Japan, yielding no immediate commissions for Takada and fading into obscurity amid the era's aggressive percussion trends.[5] It represented a deliberate counterpoint to virtuosic display, emphasizing meditative repetition and cross-cultural synthesis as her signature, though commercial breakthrough came decades later via 2017 reissues on WRWTFWW and Palto Flats, fueled by YouTube virality that introduced it to global audiences and spurred tours.[5][18] Critics later hailed it as a "holy grail" of Japanese ambient minimalism for its assimilation of global modes into cohesive, spiritually resonant forms.[18][22]Mid-Career Collaborations and Developments
Following the release of Through the Looking Glass in 1983, Takada shifted focus toward diverse collaborations and interdisciplinary projects, reflecting her deepening interest in global percussion traditions amid financial challenges that had previously disbanded the Mkwaju Ensemble. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, she engaged in cross-cultural exchanges, studying and performing with musicians from Africa and Asia to integrate non-Western rhythmic structures into her minimalist framework.[19][23] A pivotal collaboration occurred in 1990 with Ghanaian gyil (xylophone) master Kakraba Lobi, resulting in the album African Percussion Meeting, which juxtaposed Japanese marimba techniques against West African polyrhythms in improvisational duets emphasizing timbre and repetition.[24][19] Takada also partnered with Senegalese griot Lamine Konté, the Burkinabé ensemble Farafina, and Korean kayagum player Chi Seong-ja, producing recordings that highlighted acoustic resonances between Eastern and African instruments without electronic augmentation.[23][6] These efforts stemmed from her self-directed studies of field recordings and live instruction, prioritizing organic percussion dialogues over fusion stylization.[19] Domestically, Takada composed original scores and performed live for theater productions directed by Tadashi Suzuki, beginning in the mid-1980s and continuing through the 1990s with his Suzuki Company of Toga; these works adapted her repetitive motifs to dramatic pacing, influencing her shift toward more performative, site-specific minimalism.[5][25] Concurrently, she joined the improvisational ensemble Ton-Klami for experimental sessions blending jazz elements with percussion improvisation.[6] In 1990, Takada released Lunar Cruise, a studio collaboration with jazz pianist and composer Masahiko Satoh, featuring marimba layered over piano and subtle synth textures to evoke nocturnal, ethereal landscapes in six tracks averaging five minutes each.[26][27] Throughout this period, Takada balanced performance with academia, teaching percussion and composition at Tokyo universities, where she emphasized technical precision in non-tempered scales drawn from her travels.[23] These activities sustained her career amid limited commercial releases, fostering innovations in live ensemble dynamics that prefigured her later solo evolutions.[28]Tree of Life and Later Solo Works
Tree of Life, Midori Takada's second solo album, was recorded in September 1998 at Onkio Haus studio in Ginza, Tokyo.[29] [30] The album comprises 12 tracks, including "Love Song Of Urfa" (2:45), "Tan Tejah" (8:21), "Tayurani" (7:43), and "Wa-Na-Imba" (4:08), totaling approximately 46 minutes.[31] [32] It was initially released on CD exclusively in Japan in 1999 by BAJ Records, characterized by minimalist percussion and ambient elements.[33] [34] In November 2022, WRWTFWW Records issued a worldwide vinyl edition, featuring half-speed mastering on 180-gram vinyl and remixing/remastering supervised by Takada herself.[34] [35] [36] Following a 23-year gap in new solo releases, Takada issued Cutting Branches For A Temporary Shelter on June 10, 2022, via WRWTFWW Records in collaboration with MEG Museum, Geneva.[37] [38] The album includes tracks such as "Cutting Branches For A Temporary Shelter (In the Morning)" and others emphasizing her percussion-driven approach.[37] This release marked a return to solo composition, building on Takada's established minimalist style with ambient and rhythmic explorations.[39] No additional solo albums followed immediately after, though Takada continued collaborative projects in the interim.[30]Recent Career and Global Revival
Following the 2017 reissue of her 1983 album Through the Looking Glass by Japanese label Nous'klaer Audio, Takada experienced a significant resurgence in international recognition, driven initially by viral dissemination on platforms like YouTube, where tracks garnered millions of streams and introduced her minimalist percussion work to younger audiences.[5][40] This digital revival prompted reissues of other catalog material, including Tree of Life (1999), and elevated her profile beyond niche experimental circles.[41] Takada capitalized on this momentum with live performances across Europe and Asia, including sold-out concerts at London's Barbican Centre and appearances at festivals, marking a departure from her earlier, more sporadic touring.[23] In 2022, at age 70, she released two new solo albums on the Swiss label WRWTFWW Records: You Who Are Leaving to Nirvana, featuring ethereal, loop-based compositions with sho (Japanese mouth organ) and percussion, and Cutting Branches for a Temporary Shelter, emphasizing sparse, nature-inspired improvisations recorded in a Kyoto forest.[42] These works, her first original full-length releases in over two decades, received praise for maintaining her signature blend of repetition and spatial acoustics while adapting to contemporary recording techniques.[3] By 2025, Takada's global appeal continued to expand through high-profile collaborations, notably with Danish guitarist Jakob Bro on the duo album Until I Met You (released September 2025 on ECM Records), which fused her rhythmic precision with Bro's jazz minimalism during joint performances, including a Tokyo residency organized by EACH STORY in October.[43] This partnership, alongside ongoing solo and ensemble dates, underscores her sustained activity into her mid-70s, with no signs of retirement amid Japan's cultural norm of lifelong artistic engagement.[3] Her revived catalog has since influenced ambient and experimental genres, evidenced by citations in peer discussions and streaming data exceeding prior benchmarks.[44]Musical Style and Influences
Percussion Techniques and Minimalist Composition
Takada employs a wide array of percussion instruments, including marimba, vibraphone, xylophones, gongs, bells from Indian and Japanese traditions, horse bells, and Balinese wooden elements, often layering them through overdubbing to build dense sonic textures.[41][45] She incorporates extended techniques with found objects such as grass, stones, seeds, leaves, metal chopsticks, glass bowls, Coca-Cola bottles, and even iron sculptures, striking them to evoke organic or improvised resonances that emphasize acoustic purity over electronic manipulation.[41][19] Her playing style features virtuoso precision and meditative control, with rapid shifts between instruments like drums, cymbals, and marimba, creating a hypnotic, polyrhythmic flow that prioritizes tonal clarity and spatial dynamics.[41][3][46] In her minimalist compositions, Takada draws on interlocking patterns and phased repetitions akin to Steve Reich's early works, such as Clapping Music, adapting them to percussion ensembles for gradual, process-driven evolution rather than dramatic climaxes.[45][19] She integrates rhythms from African traditions, including those of the Gogo and Zanaki tribes learned via field recordings and studies with Ghanaian musicians like Kakraba Lobi, arranging them for marimba to produce trance-like, hypnotic cycles that evoke dream states.[41][19] This approach, refined in works like the 1983 album Through the Looking Glass—which she self-recorded in two days using analogue tape and precise microphone placement for three-dimensional depth—treats percussion as a "sound canvas" for spiritual immersion, blending minimal repetition with subtle atmospheric variations.[45][19][5] Takada's method demands mental discipline, viewing minimalism as a framework for non-emotive, body-centered expression that avoids machine-like uniformity, instead fostering organic phasing and textural buildup through live or multi-tracked performance.[41][19] In ensemble settings like the Mkwaju Ensemble, formed in 1981, she orchestrates polyrhythms across marimbas and gongs, drawing from Asian and African sources to create steady grids of beats that prioritize endurance and subtle harmonic shifts over tempo changes.[19][45] This technique, evident in tracks like "Mr. Henri Rousseau's Dream," intersperses slow marimba motifs with gong sustains, yielding a contemplative minimalism that integrates cultural rhythms without overt fusion, grounded in acoustic immediacy.[4][47]Cross-Cultural Integrations and Innovations
Takada's compositional approach prominently features the fusion of Japanese taiko and percussion traditions with African polyrhythms, which she explored through field recordings from Tanzania and Zimbabwe as well as direct study of drumming techniques in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.[5][48] This integration is evident in her emphasis on cross-rhythmic structures, where interlocking African-inspired beats overlay sparse Japanese minimalist frameworks, creating hypnotic layers that prioritize repetition and subtle timbral shifts over harmonic progression.[16][49] A key innovation lies in her adaptation of Indonesian gamelan principles—studied during time in Bali—into ensemble works, where metallophone and gong elements from gamelan merge with African percussion to form cyclical, environmental soundscapes that evoke natural resonance rather than narrative development.[48][21] In albums like Kiachang and Mkwaju (both 1981) with the Mkwaju Ensemble, Takada orchestrated these elements to produce minimalist compositions that blend the intricate delicacy of gamelan with the propulsive energy of African drumming, resulting in pieces that function as meditative rituals blending Eastern and non-Western traditions.[25] Her solo debut Through the Looking Glass (1983) further innovates by layering solo marimba and vibraphone with echoed African rhythms and gamelan-like ostinatos, crafting an ambient idiom that anticipates global electronic minimalism while grounding it in acoustic, culturally hybrid percussion.[49][21][50] These cross-cultural syntheses represent a deliberate departure from Western classical rigidity, which Takada critiqued for fostering aggression over introspection, toward a percussion-centric universality that draws on the bodily immediacy of African and Southeast Asian forms to innovate within Japanese experimental music.[25][51] Later works, such as collaborations incorporating sho and folk percussion, extend this by evoking timeless human sonic practices across continents, though her core innovation remains the economical use of limited instruments to generate expansive, trance-inducing textures.[52][53]Other Artistic Contributions
Theatrical Compositions
Takada has composed original scores for theatrical productions directed by Tadashi Suzuki, integrating her percussive techniques into live performances with the Suzuki Company of Toga.[25] These collaborations, spanning from the 1980s through recent decades, emphasize atmospheric soundscapes tailored to Suzuki's dramatic style.[5][54] In the past two decades, Takada has prioritized theater over concert halls, creating and performing live music for stage works by directors including Yukio Ninagawa and Suzuki.[23] Her theatrical compositions draw on minimalist principles and cross-cultural percussion elements, supporting narrative tension without overshadowing dialogue or movement.[6] Specific scores remain largely unrecorded, focusing instead on site-specific improvisation and ensemble integration during rehearsals and runs.[30]Film Scores and Multimedia Work
Takada has contributed percussion performances to several film and video game soundtracks, enhancing their atmospheric and rhythmic elements through her minimalist style. In the 2016 film Shin Godzilla, directed by Hideaki Anno and Shinji Higuchi, she provided additional percussion for select tracks composed primarily by Shiro Sagisu, as credited on the official soundtrack release.[55] Similarly, for the 2002 anime series Haibane Renmei, Takada performed percussion on the soundtrack Hanenone, arranged by Kow Otani, contributing to its introspective and ethereal tone.[56] Her percussion work appears in multiple entries of the Final Fantasy franchise, including Final Fantasy X (2001), where she played on tracks amid Nobuo Uematsu's orchestral score; Final Fantasy XI (2002); and Final Fantasy XII (2006).[57][58] In multimedia contexts, Takada has composed original scores that integrate her signature ambient percussion with visual narratives. For the 2022 audiovisual installation TOKINOKAWA ("River of Time"), presented at the British Film Institute as part of the Japan on Film series, she created a bespoke electronic score accompanying AI-reprocessed archival footage from early 20th-century Japanese cinema (1902–1913), emphasizing themes of time, memory, and cultural flux across six screens in immersive surround sound.[59] The work blends her minimalist compositions with sound design by Tim Cowie, drawing on recordings made in Japan in 2020. Additionally, Takada collaborated with vocalist Lafawndah on Le Renard Bleu (2018), a multimedia project including an original score for a short film directed by Partel Oliva for the Kenzo fashion house, fusing ambient electronics, percussion, and vocal elements into a cinematic soundscape.[60] Takada has also performed live multimedia accompaniments, improvising percussion scores for silent or archival films to evoke meditative responses. At events such as the 2023 Rewire Festival's "Japan on Film" presentation, she provided real-time musical interpretations of historical Japanese footage, extending her practice of merging composition with visual media. These efforts highlight her role in bridging traditional percussion techniques with contemporary installation art and experimental cinema.[61]Reception and Legacy
Initial Commercial and Critical Response
Midori Takada's initial recordings with the Mkwaju Ensemble, released in 1981 on the avant-garde label Better Days, garnered modest attention within Japan's experimental music scene but achieved no significant commercial breakthrough or widespread critical acclaim.[62] The ensemble's hybrid of African, Asian, and minimalist percussion elements appealed to niche audiences interested in non-Western rhythmic explorations, yet lacked broader market penetration or chart performance.[5] Her debut solo album, Through the Looking Glass (1983), fared similarly, with production limited to approximately 2,000 vinyl copies that resulted in sales so negligible they disappointed the releasing label, leading to disinterest in further projects.[4][63] Critically, the album sank without trace upon release, resonating only with a small cadre of listeners attuned to its introspective, multi-tracked percussion and spatial sound design, rather than attracting mainstream reviewers or endorsements.[25] Takada herself reflected that her music was "not popular" during this period, reflecting a broader context of limited opportunities for female composers in Japan's 1980s avant-garde landscape, where experimental works often remained confined to underground circuits without institutional or media amplification.[5] This initial obscurity contrasted with the ensemble and solo efforts' technical innovation, underscoring a disconnect between artistic intent and contemporary reception.[25]Modern Revival and Achievements
The 2017 reissue of Takada's 1983 album Through the Looking Glass by the labels WRWTFWW and Palto Flats marked a pivotal point in her modern revival, transforming the once-obscure recording into a global phenomenon among ambient and minimalist music enthusiasts.[18] The reissue received Pitchfork's designation as Best New Reissue, highlighting its assimilation of global musical modes through percussion, and propelled the album to become the second best-selling release of 2017 on Discogs, behind only Radiohead's OK Computer.[5] This surge was amplified by viral YouTube uploads and social media sharing, which introduced her work to younger generations and established it as a cult favorite comparable to influences like Brian Eno and Steve Reich.[3] The reissues, including Lunar Cruise (1990) that same year, prompted Takada's return to international stages after a period of relative seclusion.[23] She undertook a successful European tour in 2017, featuring sold-out performances such as at London's Café Oto, where her percussive sets blended serene minimalism with theatrical intensity.[19] Subsequent appearances included venues like the Barbican in London, Palais de Tokyo in Paris, and Hebbel am Ufer in Berlin, alongside festival slots at Rising in Melbourne (2022) and WOS in Santiago de Compostela (September 17, 2023), often incorporating multimedia elements like Japanese film footage.[23][4] In recent years, Takada has expanded into interdisciplinary collaborations, such as composing three pieces for a Bottega Veneta installation at V&A Dundee in Scotland, underscoring her enduring influence in ambient music's resurgence.[4] Despite the COVID-19 pandemic interrupting live work around 2020, her pre- and post-pandemic tours across Europe, the US, and Australia have solidified her reputation as a virtuoso performer active into her later career, with original vinyl copies of her early works now fetching up to $960 on resale markets.[3][4]Assessments of Limitations and Criticisms
Takada's compositions, particularly in the minimalist and ambient genres, have faced scant artistic criticism in available reviews, which predominantly emphasize their hypnotic precision and innovative percussion layering over any perceived shortcomings.[18][64] One noted limitation lies in the repetitive structures inherent to her style, which, while intentional for meditative effect, may constrain dynamic variation in longer pieces, as observed in general minimalist critiques but not uniquely attributed to her work in specific analyses.[65] Commercially, her 1983 debut solo album Through the Looking Glass sold poorly at initial release, limiting its dissemination and influence until a 2017 reissue catalyzed wider recognition via digital platforms.[5] This obscurity persisted through the 1990s and early 2000s, with original pressings becoming prohibitively expensive for collectors and her catalog largely unavailable outside compilations or Japan.[18] Her discographic output has been intermittent, spanning collaborations and solo efforts over four decades without consistent prolificacy, which some observers attribute to her focus on live performance and theatrical integrations rather than studio production.[66] This sporadic release pattern, while allowing for refined craftsmanship, has constrained opportunities for sustained critical discourse or evolutionary assessment during career gaps.[44]Discography
Solo Albums
Takada's debut solo album, Through the Looking Glass, was released in 1983 and features minimalist percussion compositions incorporating repetitive rhythms and ambient elements inspired by Japanese and global traditions.[21] Originally issued on the Soundscape label, it remained obscure until reissues in the 2010s brought wider attention.[5] Her second solo album, Tree of Life, followed in 1999 as a CD-only release in Japan, recorded in September 1998 at Onkio Haus studio in Tokyo.[33] [67] The album includes six tracks blending percussion with melodic motifs, such as "Love Song of Urfa" and "Modoki 1 (Futa-Aya-Asobi)", emphasizing organic, evolving soundscapes.[34] It received its first vinyl edition in 2022 via WRWTFWW Records.[68] No additional solo albums were released between 1983 and 1999 or immediately after, with subsequent works primarily collaborative or compositional for other media.[30] [20]Collaborative Albums
